name: David Kowalski

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start: tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on a paramedic science degree. Mondays and Tuesdays are lectures, mostly anatomy and emergency care, and Thursdays we do simulations with a dummy in a mock ambulance. I rent a room in a shared house with two lads from the rugby club. I grew up in a village, and every Saturday I work at a hardware store, mostly loading timber and cutting keys. Dad's a mechanic and he pays part of my rent. I go home most Sundays for church and Mum's dinner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called "AI Plateau". Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, that's how I'd expect it. Machines are fine for small jobs, but people still do the real work. I'd tell the lads that you can't learn paramedic work from a screen, and I'd say that to anyone who'd listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately it suits me. I don't use any AI and I don't plan to. I don't trust it with something like a patient's heartbeat. But I'm still worried about debt, because the loan is a lot for someone who didn't get top grades and hasn't got a scholarship.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am. I'd keep the hardware store shifts, about 10 hours a week, and put 25 away. I'd go on ride-alongs with the ambulance service whenever they let me. And I'd stay in the rugby club because it keeps me fit, which the job needs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady. A bit stiff in the shoulders about money, but fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which cost on your list worries you most while you study, and what would you do if money got tighter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Money's the one. Dad's garage has been quiet, and some of what he does, like diagnostics, is done by computers now. If he cut my rent share I'd take on a second Saturday job, and rugby and study would suffer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Think about the day you finish your degree. What do you picture yourself doing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I picture a night shift, a call to a road accident, and me kneeling next to someone who's frightened, doing what I was trained to do. It's good, steady work and people respect it. The pay's not great at first, but there's a pension.

say: I'd say you can't learn paramedic work from a **screen**.
I'd tell the lads machines are fine for **small jobs**, but people do the real work.
think: I don't use AI and don't plan to, because I don't trust it with a **heartbeat**.
The **loan** worries me, since I didn't get top grades or a scholarship.
do: Keep the **hardware store** shifts at about 10 hours.
Go on **ride-alongs** with the ambulance service whenever allowed.
feel: **Steady**, with a bit of stiffness over money.
S0.quote: You can't learn paramedic work from a screen, and I'd say that to anyone who'd listen.
fieldNote: David is **comfortable** with a plateau because it fits his habits.
His real worry is the **loan** and his dad's quiet garage.

steps.text: Keep the Saturday shifts at the hardware store
Book ride-alongs with the ambulance service

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called "Steady Disruption". Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's overblown for people like us. Paper jobs, sure, they'll shrink. But a man in a field, or a paramedic in a ditch, isn't replaced by software. I'd say the government should stop panicking and keep apprenticeships going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm a bit tense. Dispatch and records are going to software, and I know that. The hands-on part is safe for years. But Dad's garage depends on customers who work in offices, and the hardware store has a new stock system that makes mistakes sometimes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on. I'd keep learning the practical side and ignore the chatbots. If the ambulance service brings in new software I'd learn it when I have to, and not before. I'd stay close to the old crews, because they know what works and they're the ones who'll help me find a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly okay. A bit unsure, because the pace seems to be set by people who've never carried a stretcher.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which jobs in your field, or the part-time work you do now, would AI touch first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The hardware store would feel it first. They've got a till that does most of the ordering. The manager says Saturday staff are the ones who'd go if it works. That's my shifts, about 10 hours, so I'd have to find something else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would this change what you study, or how you study it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't change what I study. If anything I'd put more into the practical parts, like driving and first aid. The lecturers keep saying the future is data, but I think the future is someone turning up at your door.

say: I'd say a **paramedic** in a ditch isn't replaced by software.
I'd say the government should keep **apprenticeships** going.
think: Dispatch and records go to software, but the **hands-on part** is safe for years.
Dad's **garage** depends on office workers, and the store's stock system makes mistakes.
do: Keep learning the **practical** side and ignore chatbots.
Learn new ambulance **software** only when I have to.
Stay close to the **old crews** who will help me find a job.
feel: **Mostly okay**, though the pace is set by people who've never carried a stretcher.
S1.quote: The lecturers keep saying the future is data, but I think the future is someone turning up at your door.
fieldNote: David thinks the **hands-on** core of his job is safe.
He distrusts the **pace** set by distant people.
The store's till and stock system threaten his Saturday shifts.

steps.text: Keep working at the store while shifts last
Learn ambulance software only when the service needs it
Ask the old crews about jobs after graduation

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called "AGI by 2028". Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this isn't right. I'd say the government should step in. I'd say it plainly in the pub and at church. Two years isn't a plan, it's a shock, and families and small towns will be the ones who pay for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm properly worried. If thinking jobs go in two years, people in offices lose money, Dad's garage loses customers, and the village shop shuts. My course would be fine for about three more years because of the hands-on work, but the ambulance service might not have the budget to hire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go home and talk to Dad and Mum. I'd ask the ambulance service straight out whether they're hiring. I'd cut my costs, and I'd take as many hardware hours as they'd give me. And I'd think about whether to finish the degree or go into an apprenticeship as an ambulance technician.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, and a bit angry. It feels like it's being done to ordinary people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your family, and what would you do about your degree place and your loan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop going out and I'd sell my guitar. I'd ask Dad whether the garage can keep going another year, and what he'd do if it can't. I'd talk to the minister at church too, because people in the village would all be in the same boat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only two years, who or what would you lean on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd lean on family, the church and the rugby lads. I'd lean on the ambulance service, if they'd have me. I wouldn't lean on the government, because they don't help until it's too late.

say: I'd say two years isn't a plan, it's a **shock**.
I'd say families and small towns will **pay** for it.
think: If thinking jobs go, **Dad's garage** loses customers and the village shop shuts.
My course is safe about three years, but the ambulance **budget** may not be.
do: Ask the ambulance service **straight out** whether they're hiring.
Take as many **hardware** hours as they'd give me.
Think about an **apprenticeship** as an ambulance technician.
feel: **Anxious** and a bit angry, as if it's being done to ordinary people.
S2.quote: Two years isn't a plan, it's a shock, and families and small towns will be the ones who pay for it.
fieldNote: David's worry is the **village** as much as himself.
He thinks of an **apprenticeship** over the degree.
He would turn to church and family before government.

steps.text: Ask the ambulance service if they're hiring
Cut spending and sell the guitar
Talk to Dad about how long the garage can last

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called "AGI by 2031". Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives people a fair chance if they're sensible. I'd tell the lads to learn a trade or a service job. And I'd say don't depend on the government for it, get yourself a skill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be concerned but I'd have a plan. I'd graduate in 2029 and the AGI date is 2031, but hands-on work like mine lasts till about 2034. I'd have a few good years as a paramedic. But Dad's garage and the village would feel it much sooner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree and work hard. I'd save about 60 a week and pay the loan down where I could. I'd try to get hired by the ambulance service straight away, and I'd stay in the rugby club for the contacts. And I'd tell Dad to think about selling the garage before it's worth nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's better than two years, but it still looks like a squeeze.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do differently in those five years compared with the two-year picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years I'd be scrambling and might leave my degree. With five years I'd finish and I'd be in a job when it hits, with a ticket in my pocket.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: At what point would you decide to stay on your course or change it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd decide after my first long placement. If the service is hiring, I'm in. If it isn't, I'd look at fire service or an apprenticeship in a trade, something that needs a person with a van and hands.

I'd tell the lads to get a **skill** and not depend on government.
think: Hands-on work like mine lasts until about **2034**, so I'd have good paramedic years.
**Dad's garage** and the village would feel it much sooner.
do: Finish the degree and aim to be **hired** straight away.
Save about **60 a week** and pay the loan down.
Tell Dad to think about **selling** the garage early.
feel: **Uneasy**, better than two years but still a squeeze.
S3.quote: With five years I'd finish and I'd be in a job when it hits, with a ticket in my pocket.
fieldNote: David's **plan** is built on hands-on work lasting longer.
He sets his decision after the first long **placement**.
He worries more about **Dad's garage** than about himself.

steps.text: Apply to the ambulance service before graduating
Save 60 a week and pay down the loan
Tell Dad to consider selling the garage early

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called "AGI by 2036". Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, and I'd say people worry too much. I'd tell the lads to work hard, look after family, and take any chance to learn a trade. In ten years half of this talk will be forgotten.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be settled. I'd be 29, with eight years in a paramedic job and my own place. Robots for hands-on work come about 2039. I'd probably be in a senior role by then, or training new people. Dad would be retired and the garage sold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree and take a job with the ambulance service. I'd buy a small house in the village and put money in a pension. I'd stay close to my family and the church. And I'd keep ignoring chatbots until I'm forced to use them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It feels like a normal working life with a warning built in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does having ten years let you do that two years wouldn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years lets me do it the proper way: degree, job, house, family. Two years doesn't let me do any of it. A decade means I can still plan to marry and settle down in the village.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a friend who's thinking of starting your degree next year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell a friend to go for it, because people will always call an ambulance. I'd say learn the real skills, not just the theory. Pick a place and a community, because that's what holds when everything else moves.

say: I'd say people worry too much, because in ten years half this **talk** will be forgotten.
I'd tell the lads to work hard and look after **family**.
think: I'd be 29 with eight years as a **paramedic**, perhaps training new people.
**Dad** would be retired and the garage sold.
do: Finish the degree and join the **ambulance service**.
Buy a small **house** in the village and start a pension.
Stay close to **family** and the church.
feel: **Calm**, like a normal working life with a warning built in.
S4.quote: Pick a place and a community, because that's what holds when everything else moves.
fieldNote: David links ten years to a **settled life**: degree, job, house, family.
His beliefs about **community** and family shape every answer.
He still plans to ignore chatbots until forced.

steps.text: Join the ambulance service after graduating
Buy a small house in the village

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because families and small towns wouldn't have time to adjust, and the garage and village shop would go first. What would help is honest information, apprenticeships that keep going, and the ambulance service saying clearly that it's hiring.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people like me aren't against change, we just don't like being told what to think about it. I'd like a straight answer from someone who's actually done the job.

headlineQuote: People like me aren't against change, we just don't like being told what to think about it.
portrait: David is a **paramedic science** first-year, 19, in a shared house, from a village.
His dad is a **mechanic**, and David works Saturdays at a hardware store and goes to church.
He is traditional and resistant, uses no AI tools, and trusts **hands-on** work and community.
He sees his own course as safe for years but fears for his dad's **garage** and the village.
His mood is uneasy in slow worlds and anxious when AGI is two or five years away.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture, because small towns, the garage and the village shop would have no time.
whatWouldHelp: Honest **information**, apprenticeships that keep going and clear hiring from the ambulance service.
